text: Teams increasingly need to support more than one quantum SDK — comparing results across them, or because different hardware partners require different toolchains. Doing this without the architecture from the last two lessons produces an unmaintainable mess of SDK-specific branches threaded through every function.

This lesson covers why Qiskit and a Q-sharp or QDK toolchain can't share a process the way the backend-abstraction pattern's Python implementations do, the SDK-adapter pattern as one more layer of abstraction, how to represent a circuit result in an SDK-neutral format for comparison, and where this pattern is worth the added complexity and where it isn't.

Lesson eleven's backend interface works because a local simulator and an IBM hardware backend are both ordinary Python objects using Qiskit underneath — they can live in the same process, the same virtual environment. Q-sharp is fundamentally different: it compiles through its own dotNET-based toolchain with its own package ecosystem, which lesson three already flagged as needing an isolated environment. You can't simply write a Q-sharp backend class that imports qsharp alongside qiskit in the same file as a Qiskit-based backend.

The fix is one more layer above the backend abstraction: an SDK adapter that represents running a logical circuit on a given SDK as a black-box operation, typically via a subprocess call, returning results in a shared, SDK-neutral format — a dataclass holding counts, shot count, SDK name, and SDK version. The Q-sharp adapter delegates to a separate virtual environment running a standalone script rather than importing qsharp in-process. The subprocess boundary is deliberate: the main process's dependency tree never has to reconcile Qiskit's and Q-sharp's packages.

Because both adapters return the same neutral result shape, cross-SDK comparison reuses the statistical-testing toolkit from Chapter 2 directly — it's just asking whether two count distributions are statistically consistent with each other, instead of one sample against a theoretical expectation.

This pattern adds real overhead — process boundaries, a neutral result format, two separate environments to maintain. It's worth it when you have a genuine, ongoing need to run the same logical algorithm across SDKs. It is not worth it for a project that only ever targets one SDK — don't build the adapter layer speculatively in case you need a second SDK later. Add it when a second SDK is an actual, current requirement.
Next lesson is a hands-on lab: take a single tangled does-everything function and refactor it through every layer this chapter has built, then verify the refactor didn't change behavior.
